front.title: Media Keys for Calls in More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI)

abstract.t: A MIMI room is an MLS group, and MLS can give an application a secret derived from that group. A call among the room's members could take its media keys from there, which would make the call end-to-end encrypted with no key agreement of its own. This document says how, and says why the shape of the room decides whether it is safe: the secret MLS exports is computable by every member of the group, so it confines a call's media only when the group is the call. It defines a MIMI application component for media keys, derives the media secret for a call whose room is its own, and describes what an implementation does instead for a call among only some of a room's members.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The MIMI drafts have the pieces of an end-to-end encrypted call and do not say that they go together.

, Section 5.10 carries the endpoint: a body part whose disposition is session holds "a description of a multimedia session, or a URI used to join one". , Section 5 describes the room: "A room can be both fixed_membership and parent_dependent, for example, for room used for a multi-media call of clients in a Group DM". , Section 4.4 supplies key material: a forward-secure exporter giving one secret per application component. , Sections 10.2 and 10.3 register application components already, so the registry a media component would live in exists.

No document joins them. Section 5.10 states that "further discussion of calling and conferencing functionality is out-of-scope of this document", and nothing else takes the subject up. An implementation can therefore assemble a keyed call out of machinery that all exists, and two implementations will not agree, because nothing says which component keys the media or what feeds it.

This document fills that gap. sets out the constraint that decides the rest: the exported secret belongs to the whole MLS group, so whether it is the right key for a call depends on whether the group is the call. A call therefore needs a room of its own, which specifies, and covers a call that has none.

section.name: Conventions and Definitions
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

A room is a MIMI room (), and the MLS group () associated with it. A call is a real-time media session among some or all of a room's participants. A participant of a call is a user whose clients are entitled to the call's media.

section.name: Why the Group Secret Is Not Always the Call Secret
section.t: , Section 4.4 defines the safe exporter. For an application component identified by a ComponentID, it gives
whose root is the application_export_secret, derived from the group's epoch_secret. Two properties of that construction matter here.

It is forward-secure. Section 4.4 requires an implementation to treat a component's exported secret as consumed and to "delete any source key material according to the deletion schedule in Section 9.2 of ". A secret recovered later does not expose an earlier call.

It is also computable by every member of the group. The function takes a ComponentID and nothing else. There is no per-call context, so a component receives one secret per epoch, and any further derivation an application performs on that secret is equally computable by every member. Entitlement to a call's media therefore cannot be established by deriving keys from the group secret. It can only be established by the membership of the group that the secret comes from.

A call among three participants of a twenty-participant room, keyed from that room's exported secret, is readable by all twenty, subject only to their obtaining the media. The seventeen who are not on the call are not attackers: they are members of the group whose key schedule produced the key, and no protocol error has occurred. The call is not confined to the people on it.
So a call keyed this way MUST be a call whose room is its own, and specifies that case. describes what an implementation does for a call that is not.

section.name: A Call in Its Own Room
The Room
section.t: A call MAY be given a room of its own. Such a room is a parent-dependent room (, Section 5) whose parent is the room the call was started from, and whose participants are the call's participants. Giving the call its own room makes the MLS group's membership and the call's entitled set the same, which requires.
A room used this way SHOULD also be fixed_membership, so that the call's participant set is settled when the call starts, which is the combination Section 5 of names.

li.t: Note: as of -04, Section 5 requires a parent-dependent room's participants to be a strict subset of the parent's, which forbids a call whose participants are all of the parent's. That is the commonest call in a small room. This document assumes the rule is a subset rather than a strict subset.

section.name: The Media Component
section.t: This document defines a MIMI application component, media_keys, whose ComponentID is registered in . The component performs no operation on the room's application data; it exists so that media key material has a ComponentID of its own, and so that the key schedule separates it from every other component by the domain separation Section 4.1 of provides.

section.name: Deriving the Media Secret
section.t: For each epoch of the call room's MLS group, a client derives
of the group's cipher suite hash length, and uses it as the input keying material of the media layer's own key schedule. A client MUST NOT use the media_secret directly as a media encryption key.

This document does not define the media layer's key schedule. has one, and a deployment using another supplies its own; in both cases media_secret is the shared input and the media layer derives from it. What this document specifies is where the shared secret comes from and who can compute it.

section.name: Rekeying
section.t: A call is rekeyed by its group rather than by anything in this document.

Every change of the MLS group's epoch changes media_secret. Adding a participant to the call is a Commit, and so is removing one, so the media key changes at each. A client MUST derive a new media_secret on entering a new epoch and MUST stop using the previous one for new media.
Two properties follow:

list.t: A participant removed from the call loses access to subsequent media at once, because the epoch they were removed in is the last one whose secret they can compute. No media-layer rekeying protocol is needed to achieve it.
A participant added to the call cannot compute the secret of any earlier epoch, so earlier media stays unreadable to them.

section.name: A Call Among a Subset of a Room
section.t: An implementation may want a call among some of a room's participants without creating a room for it. rules out the exported secret for this case. An implementation MAY instead distribute a media secret of its own choosing to the call's participants using the Safe HPKE interface of , Section 4.2:
encrypted once to each participating client's HPKE public key from the group's ratchet tree. The secret then reaches the participants and no other member of the room.

This costs what gets from MLS. The initiator must mint the secret, must distribute it again whenever the participant set changes, and must define what a client does when it receives a secret for a call it is already in. Removing a participant from a call in particular requires a fresh secret distributed to the remainder, which is a rekeying protocol this document does not specify. An implementation that wants a call to be as safe as its membership SHOULD give the call its own room.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: is a security consideration throughout.

An implementation that keys a call from a room's exported secret without giving the call its own room has built a call that every member of the room can decrypt. This is not detectable by the call's participants and produces no protocol error.

A member of the room that hosts a call room is not thereby a participant of the call: the call room is a different MLS group with a different key schedule, and membership of the parent conveys no ability to compute the child's secrets. The reverse also holds, which the room-policy relationship might not suggest: a participant of a parent-dependent room computes nothing about its parent's traffic beyond what its own membership of the parent gives it.

Media is carried outside MLS, typically through a media server that forwards it. Such a server learns who is speaking to whom and for how long whether or not it can read the media. This document does not change that, and a deployment that needs to conceal it needs more than key management.
The media_secret is key material. A client MUST NOT send it over MIMI, MUST NOT log it, and MUST discard it when it leaves the call's group.

section.name: Replacement Text for MIMI Content
section.t: If the working group takes calling into scope, this section proposes adding the following to , Section 5.10, after the sentence that puts further discussion of calling out of scope:

li.t: A session part names an endpoint; a receiver does not fetch it as it would other external content, and the size, expires, encAlg and hashAlg fields of such a part carry no meaning. Where the media of the session named by the part is to be end-to-end encrypted among the members of a MIMI room, [this document] describes how the media keys are derived from that room's MLS group.

section.name: Implementation Status
section.t: This section is to be removed before publication, per .

The argument of came out of implementing Section 5.10 in mimid, an implementation of the MIMI drafts. mimid converts a session part to and from its own front ends and does not fetch it. At the time of writing mimid implements neither the exporter of , Section 4.4 nor parent-dependent rooms, so no part of has been tested between two implementations, and this document makes no interoperability claim.

abstract.t: Messaging applications are increasingly making use of end-to-end security mechanisms to ensure that messages are only accessible to the communicating endpoints, and not to any servers involved in delivering messages. Establishing keys to provide such protections is challenging for group chat settings, in which more than two clients need to agree on a key but may not be online at the same time. In this document, we specify a key establishment protocol that provides efficient asynchronous group key establishment with forward secrecy (FS) and post-compromise security (PCS) for groups in size ranging from two to thousands.

front.title: More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI) using HTTPS and MLS

abstract.t: This document specifies the More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI) transport protocol, which allows users of different messaging providers to interoperate in group chats (rooms), including to send and receive messages, share room policy, and add participants to and remove participants from rooms. MIMI describes messages between providers, leaving most aspects of the provider-internal client- server communication up to the provider. MIMI integrates the Messaging Layer Security (MLS) protocol to provide end-to-end security assurances, including authentication of protocol participants, confidentiality of messages exchanged within a room, and agreement on the state of the room.

front.title: More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI) message content

abstract.t: This document describes content semantics common in Instant Messaging (IM) systems and describes a profile suitable for instant messaging interoperability of messages end-to-end encrypted inside the MLS (Message Layer Security) Protocol.

front.title: Room Policy for the More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI) Protocol

abstract.t: This document describes a set of concrete room policies for the More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI) Working Group. It describes several independent properties and policy attributes which can be combined to model a wide range of chat and multimedia conference types.

The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) protocol is an asynchronous group authenticated key exchange protocol. MLS provides a number of capabilities to applications, as well as several extension points internal to the protocol. This document provides a consolidated application API, guidance for how the protocol's extension points should be used, and a few concrete examples of both core protocol extensions and uses of the application API.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

This document describes a scheme for hybrid public key encryption (HPKE). This scheme provides a variant of public key encryption of arbitrary-sized plaintexts for a recipient public key. It also includes three authenticated variants, including one that authenticates possession of a pre-shared key and two optional ones that authenticate possession of a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) private key. HPKE works for any combination of an asymmetric KEM, key derivation function (KDF), and authenticated encryption with additional data (AEAD) encryption function. Some authenticated variants may not be supported by all KEMs. We provide instantiations of the scheme using widely used and efficient primitives, such as Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key agreement, HMAC-based key derivation function (HKDF), and SHA2.
This document is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG) in the IRTF.

front.title: Improving Awareness of Running Code: The Implementation Status Section

abstract.t: This document describes a simple process that allows authors of Internet-Drafts to record the status of known implementations by including an Implementation Status section. This will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature.

This process is not mandatory. Authors of Internet-Drafts are encouraged to consider using the process for their documents, and working groups are invited to think about applying the process to all of their protocol specifications. This document obsoletes RFC 6982, advancing it to a Best Current Practice.

This document describes the Secure Frame (SFrame) end-to-end encryption and authentication mechanism for media frames in a multiparty conference call, in which central media servers (selective forwarding units or SFUs) can access the media metadata needed to make forwarding decisions without having access to the actual media.
The proposed mechanism differs from the Secure Real-Time Protocol (SRTP) in that it is independent of RTP (thus compatible with non-RTP media transport) and can be applied to whole media frames in order to be more bandwidth efficient.
